sections.label: The opening
sections.line: How much to let go depends on undo cost
sections.para: The newsroom released fourteen times in one day unapproved, while every email still waits for me. The test is how cheap an output is to undo: email is a one-way door with young controls, the newsroom a two-way door with mature ones. Both the cost of undoing and control maturity move over time.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Auto-release suits two-way doors with mature controls
sections.para: An email cannot be claimed back and its workflow is young, so it waits for me. An article is corrected as a new version, few read it yet, and validators, tests, leak scans and a reader who has never pulled a piece guard it. Readership and maturing controls keep moving the line.

sections.label: What we noticed
sections.line: We arrived at auto-release without ever deciding to
sections.para: Writing The human in the loop surfaced an unplanned contrast: on 13 October the newsroom released fourteen times with every commit by an agent and no approval, while agents draft every email and I send each one. Nobody designed it, and it shows trust and control form a spectrum, not a switch.

sections.label: The test: how cheap is it to undo?
sections.line: Ask how cheap an output is to undo
sections.para: A remembered executive, probably at Google, approved experiments that could be switched off with little side effect. Bezos's 2015 letter separates one-way from two-way doors, and Google's SRE book says roughly 70% of outages come from changes, answered by safe rollback. The agent question becomes what breaks before an output is undone.

sections.label: Email is a one-way door, and still an explorer
sections.line: Email is a one-way door still in exploration
sections.para: A sent email cannot be recalled, and a wrong fact, tone or duplicate damages a relationship immediately. The workflow is still in the explorer phase: the second reader was built after two emails went wrong, the rest is policy and me, and there is no long record of unchanged sends yet.

sections.label: The newsroom is a two-way door, with mature controls
sections.line: Articles are two-way doors guarded by mature controls
sections.para: A correction is a new version with a diff page, few people read yet, and new articles land in the latest list without front-page placement, still the 8 October edition. A validator, browser tests, leak scans and briefing packs guard releases, and I have never read an article and wanted it pulled.

sections.label: Two axes, and both move
sections.line: Undo cost and control maturity decide, and both move
sections.para: One axis is the cost of undoing, the other the maturity of controls and record, from explorer to villager to town planner. Growing readership will raise the newsroom's side effects, while maturing controls let email types leave my hands by written, owned decisions. Decide by output, not department, and revisit.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Small readership and one reader's record shape this
sections.para: The newsroom's low side effects partly reflect few readers, so scale would need a canary stage. Never pulling an article is my record over a few weeks, not a measurement. A leaked key is a one-way door, hence the pre-commit scan, and the Google executive is a memory, not a source.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: a voice memo, Bezos's letter, Google SRE
sections.para: The article came from my voice memo of 13 October 2026, after reading The human in the loop. It cites Jeff Bezos's 2015 shareholder letter and Google's Site Reliability Engineering book on rollback, with release counts from the git log and front-page placement from the 8 October edition file.
